      - redis

      - DOCKER=true
      - RAILS_ENV=development

      - DATABASE_HOST=db

      args:

    volumes:
      - ./:/campaignzee
    links:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379
      - DATABASE_HOST=db
      - DATABASE_PORT=5432

      - ./:/campaignzee

require "sidekiq"
require "sidekiq/pro/expiry"
require Rails.root.join("lib", "newrelic", "newrelic_json_logger")

Sidekiq.configure_client do |config|
  # For Git Flow we use REDISCLOUD_URL for Sidekiq
  config.redis = Rails.application.config.sidekiq_client_redis_options
end

Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
  config.super_fetch!
  Platform::Database.reconnect(Integer(ENV["SIDEKIQ_CONCURRENCY"] || 20) + 1)
  config.redis = Rails.application.config.sidekiq_server_redis_options
  # Configure Sidekiq logger with JSON formatter and NewRelic metadata
  logger = ActiveSupport::Logger.new($stdout)
  logger.formatter = NewRelicJsonLogger.new
  logger.progname = "campaignzee-sidekiq"
  logger.level = Logger::WARN if Rails.env.production?
  config.logger = logger
end

::Sidekiq.default_job_options = {"backtrace" => 20} # save 20 lines of backtrace on errors

require File.expand_path("boot", __dir__)

require "rails/all"

Bundler.require(*Rails.groups(assets: %w[development test]))

module App
  class Application < Rails::Application
    require "resolv"
    require "resolv-replace"
    require "campaignzee/request_method_middleware"

    # Rails LTS
    config.rails_lts_options = {default: :hardened}

    # Initialize configuration defaults for originally generated Rails version.
    config.load_defaults 6.1

    # Don't require belongs_to associations by default.
    # This is a breaking change in Rails 5, but we have a lot of existing code that would be affected by this change and
    # we don't want to require belongs_to associations for all of our models. We can enable this on a per-model basis if needed.
    config.active_record.belongs_to_required_by_default = false

    # Settings in config/environments/* take precedence over those specified here.
    # Application configuration should go into files in config/initializers
    # -- all .rb files in that directory are automatically loaded.

    # Set Time.zone default to the specified zone and make Active Record auto-convert to this zone.
    # Run "rake -D time" for a list of tasks for finding time zone names. Default is UTC.
    # config.time_zone = 'Central Time (US & Canada)'

    # The default locale is :en and all translations from config/locales/*.rb,yml are auto loaded.
    # config.i18n.load_path += Dir[Rails.root.join('my', 'locales', '*.{rb,yml}').to_s]
    # config.i18n.default_locale = :de

    # Do not swallow errors in after_commit/after_rollback callbacks.

    config.middleware.use Campaignzee::RequestMethodMiddleware

    # Custom directories with classes and modules you want to be
    # autoloadable.
    [
      Dir[Rails.root.join("app", "queries")],
      Dir[Rails.root.join("app", "services")],
      Dir[Rails.root.join("lib", "{**}/*")]
    ].each do |autoload_paths|
      config.autoload_paths += autoload_paths
    end

    config.generators do |g|
      g.test_framework :rspec, fixture: true
      g.fixture_replacement :factory_bot, dir: "spec/factories"
      g.view_specs false
      g.helper_specs false
      g.stylesheets = false
      g.javascripts = false
      g.helper = false
    end

    # Number of seconds after which to expire cache
    config.subject_line_cache_expires_in_seconds = (ENV["SUBJECT_LINE_CACHE_EXPIRES_IN_SECONDS"] || 1.hour).to_i

    # Enable escaping HTML in JSON.
    config.active_support.escape_html_entities_in_json = true

    I18n.enforce_available_locales = false

    config.action_dispatch.perform_deep_munge = false # allow empty arrays in JSON from apis... see https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/13188
  end
end

Rails.application.configure do
  # Settings specified here will take precedence over those in config/application.rb.

  # Code is not reloaded between requests.
  config.cache_classes = true

  # Eager load code on boot. This eager loads most of Rails and
  # your application in memory, allowing both threaded web servers
  # and those relying on copy on write to perform better.
  # Rake tasks automatically ignore this option for performance.
  config.eager_load = true

  # Enable caching.
  config.action_controller.perform_caching = true

  redis_ssl_cache_params =
    if ENV["REDIS_CACHE_CLIENT_CERT"]

      # Load the certificates and private keys from environment variables
      client_cert_content = ENV["REDIS_CACHE_CLIENT_CERT"].gsub('\\n', "\n")
      client_key_content = ENV["REDIS_CACHE_CLIENT_CERT_KEY"].gsub('\\n', "\n")
      trusted_cert_content = ENV["REDIS_CACHE_TRUSTED_CERT"].gsub('\\n', "\n")

      # Write the certificate contents to temporary files (if needed)
      File.write("/tmp/client_cert.pem", client_cert_content)
      File.write("/tmp/client_key.pem", client_key_content)
      File.write("/tmp/trusted_cert.pem", trusted_cert_content)

      # redis_ssl_ca_store = OpenSSL::X509::Store.new
      # redis_ssl_ca_store.add_cert(
      #   OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.read("/tmp/trusted_cert.pem"))
      # )
      {
        ssl: true,
        ssl_params: {
          cert: OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.read("/tmp/client_cert.pem")),
          key: OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.new(File.read("/tmp/client_key.pem")),
          ca_file: "/tmp/trusted_cert.pem"
        }
      }
    end

  config.cache_store = :redis_cache_store, {
    url: ENV["RAILS_FLEXI_CACHE_REDIS_URL"] || ENV["REDIS_URL"],
    pool_size: Integer(ENV["MAX_THREADS"] || 5),
    pool_timeout: 10,
    compress: true,
    reconnect_attempts: 3
  }.merge(redis_ssl_cache_params || {})

  redis_ssl_sidekiq_params =
    if ENV["REDIS_SIDEKIQ_CLIENT_CERT"]

{"type": "create", "filePath": "/Users/dhruva/src/mindbody/campaignzee/redis/gen-certs.sh", "content": "#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Generates a self-signed CA and Redis server certificate for local
# TLS-enabled Redis used by docker-compose. Idempotent: re-running
# leaves existing certs alone unless FORCE=1 is set.

set -euo pipefail

CERT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/tls"
mkdir -p "$CERT_DIR"
cd "$CERT_DIR"

if [[ "${FORCE:-0}" != "1" ]] && [[ -f ca.crt && -f redis.crt && -f redis.key ]]; then
  echo "Certificates already exist in $CERT_DIR (set FORCE=1 to regenerate)."
  exit 0
fi

rm -f ca.key ca.crt ca.srl redis.key redis.csr redis.crt redis.cnf

# 1. Root CA
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096 >/dev/null 2>&1
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -sha256 -key ca.key -days 3650 \
  -subj "/O=campaignzee-dev/CN=campaignzee-dev-ca" \
  -out ca.crt

# 2. Redis server key + CSR with SAN covering the docker hostname and localhost
openssl genrsa -out redis.key 2048 >/dev/null 2>&1
cat > redis.cnf <<'EOF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no
[req_distinguished_name]
O = campaignzee-dev
CN = redis
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = redis
DNS.2 = localhost
IP.1  = 127.0.0.1
EOF

openssl req -new -key redis.key -out redis.csr -config redis.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in redis.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out redis.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile redis.cnf -extensions v3_req

# Redis (uid 999 inside the container) must be able to read these when mounted.
chmod 644 ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

rm -f redis.csr redis.cnf ca.srl

echo "Generated TLS material in $CERT_DIR:"
ls -l ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

# Upgrade Orchestrator

Run a fully automated, phased Ruby (and optionally Rails) upgrade from start to finish. Maintain a live task list so the user can see exactly what is done, what is in progress, and what is coming next. Pause and surface any failure clearly before asking whether to continue, retry, or abort.

## Argument Parsing

Extract from the user's arguments:
- `ruby:X.Y.Z` — required target Ruby version
- `rails:X.Y` — optional target Rails version (omit sections if not provided)

## Step 1: Detect Current Versions

```bash
ruby -v 2>/dev/null || true
cat .ruby-version 2>/dev/null
grep "^ruby " Gemfile 2>/dev/null
grep -A2 "RUBY VERSION" Gemfile.lock 2>/dev/null
bundle exec rails -v 2>/dev/null || true
grep "gem ['\"]rails['\"]" Gemfile 2>/dev/null
grep "^    rails " Gemfile.lock 2>/dev/null | head -1
git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null
```

Read `Gemfile` and `Gemfile.lock`. Record:
- `CURRENT_RUBY` — current active Ruby version
- `TARGET_RUBY` — from arguments
- `CURRENT_RAILS` — if Rails project (else "none")
- `TARGET_RAILS` — from arguments (else "none")

**Early exit:** If `CURRENT_RUBY == TARGET_RUBY` and (`TARGET_RAILS` is none OR `CURRENT_RAILS == TARGET_RAILS`), print:

```
Already at target versions (Ruby TARGET_RUBY / Rails TARGET_RAILS).
Nothing to do. Run /ruby-upgrade-toolkit:status to confirm readiness.
```

Then stop.

## Step 2: Validate Compatibility

If `rails:` argument given, verify TARGET_RUBY is compatible with TARGET_RAILS:

| Target Ruby | Min Rails | Recommended |
|-------------|-----------|-------------|
| 2.7         | 5.2       | 6.0–6.1     |
| 3.0         | 6.1       | 7.0         |
| 3.1         | 7.0       | 7.0–7.1     |
| 3.2         | 7.0.4     | 7.1         |
| 3.3         | 7.1       | 7.1–7.2     |
| 3.4         | 7.2       | 7.2–8.0     |

If incompatible, stop immediately and tell the user which combinations are valid.

## Step 3: Determine Upgrade Path

If upgrading Ruby across more than one minor version (e.g. 2.7 → 3.3), list each intermediate step:
- 2.7 → 3.0 → 3.1 → 3.2 → 3.3

Each intermediate Ruby version becomes its own phase. The test suite must be green before moving to the next intermediate step.

If upgrading Rails across more than one minor version (e.g. 6.1 → 8.0):
- 6.1 → 7.0 → 7.1 → 8.0

Each intermediate Rails version becomes its own phase.

## Step 4: Build the Task List

Using `TodoWrite`, create the **full concrete task list** before any work begins. Generate one task per sub-phase, substituting the real version numbers from the upgrade path computed in Step 3.

**Example: Ruby 2.7 → 3.3, Rails 6.1 → 8.0 (generates this exact list):**

Phase 1a — Ruby 3.0.7: activate + version pins + gem updates

## Step 2: Test Suite Baseline

# Pattern A — methods with options hash default (callers must NOT pass **hash)
echo "Pattern A — options={} method definitions:"
grep -rEn "def [a-z_]+\([^)]*[a-z_]+ = \{\}" app/ lib/ --include="*.rb" 2>/dev/null | wc -l

- Pattern A method definitions + Pattern A call sites with mismatched hash: ArgumentError in Ruby 3.0 when caller passes `connect(options)` (plain hash) to a method with `def connect(**opts)`.

No arguments — detects everything from the project state. Produces a RED/YELLOW/GREEN health report.
argument-hint: "(no arguments)"
allowed-tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep
version: 0.2.0
---

# Upgrade Status

Generate a health dashboard for the current state of the upgrade. Run this after each fix phase to confirm readiness before proceeding.

## Step 1: Detect Versions

```bash
ruby -v 2>/dev/null || echo "Ruby: unknown"
cat .ruby-version 2>/dev/null
grep "^ruby " Gemfile 2>/dev/null
bundle exec rails -v 2>/dev/null || echo "Rails: not present"
grep "load_defaults" config/application.rb 2>/dev/null || true
git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null
```

## Step 2: Test Suite

```bash
if [[ -d "spec" ]]; then
  bundle exec rspec --no-color --format progress 2>&1 | tail -10
else
  bundle exec rails test 2>&1 | tail -10 2>/dev/null || echo "No test suite found"
fi
```

## Step 3: Deprecation Warning Count

```bash
if [[ -d "spec" ]]; then
  DEPR=$(RAILS_ENV=test bundle exec rspec --no-color 2>&1 | grep -c "DEPRECATION" || true)
else
  DEPR=$(RAILS_ENV=test bundle exec rails test 2>&1 | grep -c "DEPRECATION" || true)
fi
echo "Deprecation warnings: $DEPR"
```

## Step 4: Ruby Warning Count

```bash
RUBY_WARN=$(RUBYOPT="-W:deprecated" bundle exec ruby -e "require 'bundler/setup'" 2>&1 | grep -c "warning:" || echo 0)
echo "Ruby warnings: $RUBY_WARN"
```

## Step 5: RuboCop Status

```bash
bundle exec rubocop --parallel --format json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
import sys, json
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
offenses = sum(len(f['offenses']) for f in data.get('files', []))
print(f'RuboCop offenses: {offenses}')
" 2>/dev/null || bundle exec rubocop --parallel 2>&1 | tail -3
```

## Step 6: Gem Compatibility Signal

```bash
bundle outdated 2>/dev/null | grep -cE "^\s*\*" || echo "0 outdated gems"
```

## Step 7: Zeitwerk (Rails only)

```bash
if [[ -f "config/application.rb" ]]; then
  bundle exec rails zeitwerk:check 2>&1 | grep -E "error|OK|expected" | head -5
fi
```

## Step 8: Render the Report

```
# Upgrade Status Report
Generated: [datetime]
Branch: [branch name]

## Versions
| | Current | Target |
|-|---------|--------|
| Ruby | [current] | [from .ruby-version or user context] |
| Rails | [current] | [from Gemfile or user context] |
| load_defaults | [value] | — |

## Test Suite
- Status: [PASSING / FAILING / NOT FOUND]
- [N] examples, [F] failures, [P] pending

## Warnings
- Deprecation warnings: [N]
- Ruby warnings: [N]
- RuboCop offenses: [N]

## Gem Health
- Outdated gems: [N]

## Zeitwerk (Rails only)
- [OK / N errors]

## Overall Readiness: [RED / YELLOW / GREEN]

GREEN  — Tests passing, 0 deprecation warnings, 0 RuboCop offenses
YELLOW — Tests passing but warnings or offenses remain
RED    — Test failures present — do not proceed to next phase

## Suggested Next Step
[Most actionable next step based on the report]
[Command to run]
```

# Service class for making request with frederick client
module FrederickClient::RequestService
  def self.frederick_client(location_id)
    Cerberus::Services::CerberusService.client_for_location(location_id)
  end

  def self.send_campaign_emails(campaign:, emails: nil, test: false, options: {})
    options = options.deep_symbolize_keys

    raise StandardError, "Email document required" unless campaign.email_document

    return unless test || (campaign.status != Campaign::SENT)

    call_frederick_client(campaign, emails, test, options)
  end

  def self.fail_campaign!(campaign)
    campaign.assign_attributes(status: Campaign::FAILED, failed_reason: campaign.errors.full_messages.join("; "))
    campaign.save(validate: false)
    NewRelic::Agent.notice_error(
      "Campaign Failed",
      custom_params: {location_id: campaign.location_id, campaign_id: campaign.id}
    )
  end

  def self.call_frederick_client(campaign, emails, test, options)
    Campaign.transaction do
      # Set failure status if not a test && sending status not set
      return fail_campaign!(campaign) if !test && !campaign_sending_status_updated?(campaign, options)

      frederick_client(campaign.location_id).send_campaign_emails(
        html: campaign.email_document.html,
        name: campaign.name,
        subject_line: campaign.subject_line,
        location_id: campaign.location_id,
        campaign_id: campaign.id,
        test: test,
        emails: emails,
        contact_list_names: campaign.contact_lists || [],
        shared_to_location_ids: options[:shared_to_location_ids],
        skip_owner_location: options[:skip_owner_location]
      )
    end
  end

  # returns false if creation/updation fails
  def self.campaign_sending_status_updated?(campaign, options)
    if campaign.status == Campaign::SENDING
      Rails.logger.warn("campaign_sending_status_updated: campaign_id=#{campaign.id} location_id=#{campaign.location_id} is ALREADY in SENDING state - possible duplicate worker from double-scheduling.")
    end

    location_ids = options[:shared_to_location_ids].dup
    location_ids << campaign.location_id unless options[:skip_owner_location]

    # to rollback unwanted changes
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      location_ids.each do |location_id|
        CampaignLocationDetail.find_or_create_by!(
          location_id: location_id,
          campaign_id: campaign.id
        ).update!(status: CampaignLocationDetail::SENDING)
      end
      campaign.status = Campaign::SENDING
      campaign.save!
    end

    true
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid
    false
  end

  private_class_method :campaign_sending_status_updated?
end

# Service class for making request with frederick client
module FrederickClient::RequestService
  def self.frederick_client(location_id)
    Cerberus::Services::CerberusService.client_for_location(location_id)
  end

  def self.send_campaign_emails(campaign:, emails: nil, test: false, options: {})
    options = options.deep_symbolize_keys

    raise StandardError, "Email document required" unless campaign.email_document

    return unless test || (campaign.status != Campaign::SENT)

    call_frederick_client(campaign, emails, test, options)
  end

  def self.fail_campaign!(campaign)
    campaign.assign_attributes(status: Campaign::FAILED, failed_reason: campaign.errors.full_messages.join("; "))
    campaign.save(validate: false)
    NewRelic::Agent.notice_error(
      "Campaign Failed",
      custom_params: {location_id: campaign.location_id, campaign_id: campaign.id}
    )
  end

  def self.call_frederick_client(campaign, emails, test, options)
    Campaign.transaction do
      # Set failure status if not a test && sending status not set
      return fail_campaign!(campaign) if !test && !campaign_sending_status_updated?(campaign, options)

      frederick_client(campaign.location_id).send_campaign_emails(
        html: campaign.email_document.html,
        name: campaign.name,
        subject_line: campaign.subject_line,
        location_id: campaign.location_id,
        campaign_id: campaign.id,
        test: test,
        emails: emails,
        contact_list_names: campaign.contact_lists || [],
        shared_to_location_ids: options[:shared_to_location_ids],
        skip_owner_location: options[:skip_owner_location]
      )
    end
  end

  # returns false if creation/updation fails
  def self.campaign_sending_status_updated?(campaign, options)
    if campaign.status == Campaign::SENDING
      Rails.logger.warn("campaign_sending_status_updated: campaign_id=#{campaign.id} location_id=#{campaign.location_id} is ALREADY in SENDING state - possible duplicate worker from double-scheduling.")
    end

    location_ids = options[:shared_to_location_ids].dup
    location_ids << campaign.location_id unless options[:skip_owner_location]

    # to rollback unwanted changes
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      location_ids.each do |location_id|
        CampaignLocationDetail.find_or_create_by!(
          location_id: location_id,
          campaign_id: campaign.id
        ).update!(status: CampaignLocationDetail::SENDING)
      end
      campaign.status = Campaign::SENDING
      campaign.save!
    end

    true
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid
    false
  end

  private_class_method :campaign_sending_status_updated?
end

=== gen-certs.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Generates a self-signed CA and Redis server certificate for local
# TLS-enabled Redis used by docker-compose. Idempotent: re-running
# leaves existing certs alone unless FORCE=1 is set.

set -euo pipefail

CERT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/tls"
mkdir -p "$CERT_DIR"
cd "$CERT_DIR"

if [[ "${FORCE:-0}" != "1" ]] && [[ -f ca.crt && -f redis.crt && -f redis.key ]]; then
  echo "Certificates already exist in $CERT_DIR (set FORCE=1 to regenerate)."
  exit 0
fi

rm -f ca.key ca.crt ca.srl redis.key redis.csr redis.crt redis.cnf

# 1. Root CA
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096 >/dev/null 2>&1
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -sha256 -key ca.key -days 3650 \
  -subj "/O=campaignzee-dev/CN=campaignzee-dev-ca" \
  -out ca.crt

# 2. Redis server key + CSR with SAN covering the docker hostname and localhost
openssl genrsa -out redis.key 2048 >/dev/null 2>&1
cat > redis.cnf <<'EOF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no
[req_distinguished_name]
O = campaignzee-dev
CN = redis
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = redis
DNS.2 = localhost
IP.1  = 127.0.0.1
EOF

openssl req -new -key redis.key -out redis.csr -config redis.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in redis.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out redis.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile redis.cnf -extensions v3_req

# Redis (uid 999 inside the container) must be able to read these when mounted.
chmod 644 ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

rm -f redis.csr redis.cnf ca.srl

echo "Generated TLS material in $CERT_DIR:"
ls -l ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

    feat(redis): enable TLS for local docker-compose redis
    
    Switches the local Redis container to TLS-only mode (plaintext port disabled
    via --port 0; TLS on 6379) so the local dev/test stack mirrors how production
    talks to managed Redis over rediss://.
    
    * redis/gen-certs.sh — idempotent generator for a self-signed CA + server cert
      with SAN entries for redis/localhost; outputs to redis/tls/.
    * docker-compose.yml — redis service pinned to redis:7-alpine, mounts
      ./redis/tls read-only, runs redis-server in TLS-only mode. main/sidekiq
      services point at rediss://redis:6379 and pass REDIS_CA_FILE so the
      self-signed CA is trusted.
    * config/environments/{development,test}.rb — when REDIS_URL is rediss:// and
      REDIS_CA_FILE is set, merge ssl_params: { ca_file: ... } into the Sidekiq
      client/server Redis options. Plaintext fallback URL preserved when running
      outside docker-compose.
    * .gitignore — exclude /redis/tls/ so locally generated key material is never
      committed.
    
    Verified end-to-end: redis-cli plaintext is refused; TLS PING returns PONG;
    both main and sidekiq containers successfully roundtrip Sidekiq.redis writes
    over rediss:// with the CA file mounted.

# Generates a self-signed CA and Redis server certificate for local
# TLS-enabled Redis used by docker-compose. Idempotent: re-running
# leaves existing certs alone unless FORCE=1 is set.

set -euo pipefail

CERT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/tls"
mkdir -p "$CERT_DIR"
cd "$CERT_DIR"

if [[ "${FORCE:-0}" != "1" ]] && [[ -f ca.crt && -f redis.crt && -f redis.key ]]; then
  echo "Certificates already exist in $CERT_DIR (set FORCE=1 to regenerate)."
  exit 0
fi

rm -f ca.key ca.crt ca.srl redis.key redis.csr redis.crt redis.cnf

# 1. Root CA
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096 >/dev/null 2>&1
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -sha256 -key ca.key -days 3650 \
  -subj "/O=campaignzee-dev/CN=campaignzee-dev-ca" \
  -out ca.crt

# 2. Redis server key + CSR with SAN covering the docker hostname and localhost
openssl genrsa -out redis.key 2048 >/dev/null 2>&1
cat > redis.cnf <<'EOF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no
[req_distinguished_name]
O = campaignzee-dev
CN = redis
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = redis
DNS.2 = localhost
IP.1  = 127.0.0.1
EOF

openssl req -new -key redis.key -out redis.csr -config redis.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in redis.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out redis.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile redis.cnf -extensions v3_req

# Redis (uid 999 inside the container) must be able to read these when mounted.
chmod 644 ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

rm -f redis.csr redis.cnf ca.srl

echo "Generated TLS material in $CERT_DIR:"
ls -l ca.crt redis.crt redis.key

# Generates a self-signed CA, Redis server certificate, and client certificate
# for local mTLS-enabled Redis used by docker-compose. Idempotent: re-running
# leaves existing certs alone unless FORCE=1 is set.
#
# Outputs:
#   ca.crt        — self-signed root CA
#   redis.crt/.key — server cert (SANs: redis, localhost, 127.0.0.1; serverAuth)
#   client.crt/.key — client cert for mTLS (clientAuth)

set -euo pipefail

CERT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/tls"
mkdir -p "$CERT_DIR"
cd "$CERT_DIR"

if [[ "${FORCE:-0}" != "1" ]] && \
   [[ -f ca.crt && -f redis.crt && -f redis.key && -f client.crt && -f client.key ]]; then
  echo "Certificates already exist in $CERT_DIR (set FORCE=1 to regenerate)."
  exit 0
fi

rm -f ca.key ca.crt ca.srl \
      redis.key redis.csr redis.crt redis.cnf \
      client.key client.csr client.crt client.cnf

# 1. Root CA
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096 >/dev/null 2>&1
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -sha256 -key ca.key -days 3650 \
  -subj "/O=campaignzee-dev/CN=campaignzee-dev-ca" \
  -out ca.crt

# 2. Redis server key + cert (serverAuth) with SAN covering docker + localhost
openssl genrsa -out redis.key 2048 >/dev/null 2>&1
cat > redis.cnf <<'EOF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no
[req_distinguished_name]
O = campaignzee-dev
CN = redis
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = redis
DNS.2 = localhost
IP.1  = 127.0.0.1
EOF

openssl req -new -key redis.key -out redis.csr -config redis.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in redis.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out redis.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile redis.cnf -extensions v3_req

# 3. Client key + cert (clientAuth) for mTLS — used by the app + sidekiq services
openssl genrsa -out client.key 2048 >/dev/null 2>&1
cat > client.cnf <<'EOF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
req_extensions = v3_req
prompt = no
[req_distinguished_name]
O = campaignzee-dev
CN = campaignzee-client
[v3_req]
extendedKeyUsage = clientAuth
EOF

openssl req -new -key client.key -out client.csr -config client.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out client.crt -days 3650 -sha256 \
  -extfile client.cnf -extensions v3_req

# Redis (uid 999 inside the container) and Ruby (root in our images) must be
# able to read these when mounted.
chmod 644 ca.crt redis.crt redis.key client.crt client.key

rm -f redis.csr redis.cnf client.csr client.cnf ca.srl

echo "Generated TLS material in $CERT_DIR:"
ls -l ca.crt redis.crt redis.key client.crt client.key

      - ./:/campaignzee

## 2. What `tls_retry_write_records` means

`tls_retry_write_records` is an internal OpenSSL state-machine function in
`ssl/statem/statem_lib.c` (OpenSSL 3.x). It is invoked during a **read**
when OpenSSL needs to *flush previously buffered TLS records* before it can
parse the next response — typically during:

- TLSv1.3 post-handshake messages (`NewSessionTicket`, `KeyUpdate`)
- Renegotiation in TLSv1.2 (less common)
- Partial-write recovery when an earlier write was interrupted (EAGAIN /
  EWOULDBLOCK) and now needs to complete before the read can proceed

The "failure" form (`tls_retry_write_records failure`) means the internal
write retry returned a non-recoverable error. Concrete trigger conditions:

1. **TCP socket has been closed by the peer** (FIN or RST) while OpenSSL
   still has buffered records to flush. The write fails with `EPIPE` /
   `ECONNRESET`, OpenSSL converts that into the SSL-level error.
2. **Half-closed TCP** — server sent FIN, client kernel hasn't yet
   propagated. OpenSSL tries to send a close_notify or post-handshake ACK,
   the write fails.
3. **Connection idle long enough that managed Redis closed it**, then the
   next op finds OpenSSL with state to flush against a dead socket.
4. **TLSv1.3 NewSessionTicket arriving on a long-idle connection**: server
   sends a ticket, client must process it (which may involve a write), and
   if anything is wrong with the underlying connection at that moment, the
   write retry fails permanently.

holds one Redis connection, polls every ~5s, sits idle in between. Plenty of

# Abstract base class for all sidekiq workers.

# Does some basic setup for subclasses.

# @abstract
class BaseWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker

  sidekiq_retries_exhausted { |msg| report_retries_exhausted(msg) }

  class << self
    private

    def report_retries_exhausted(msg)
      NewRelic::Agent.notice_error(
        "Failed all retries of #{msg["class"]}", custom_params: {job_args: msg["args"], error: msg["error_message"]}
      )
    end
  end

  private

  def check_for_required_keys!(options)
    self.class::REQUIRED_KEYS.each { |k| raise StandardError, "required key (#{k}) has no value" if options[k].nil? }
    true
  end
end

Reference document for the production Redis (Sidekiq) TLS connection failure
we are tracking. Captures the confirmed exception, what's been investigated,

## TL;DR

- **Bug:** `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError: SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)`
  intermittently surfaces in production Sidekiq, breaks scheduled-job
  enqueue and the job-dispatch loop.
- **Root cause:** `redis-rb 4.x`'s pure-Ruby driver routes reads through
  Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering`, which does not handle the TLSv1.3 state-machine
  recovery path (`tls_retry_write_records`) cleanly. The resulting
  `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is **not** a `Redis::BaseConnectionError` — so
  redis-rb's `ensure_connected` does not retry it; it propagates to Sidekiq.
- **Stack involved:** Ruby 3.3.10 / `redis 4.8.1` / `connection_pool 2.4.1` /
  Sidekiq 6.5.12 / newrelic_rpm 10.x / **staging Redis 6.2** (TLSv1.3
  capable, server-side `tls-protocols` decides).
- **Decision — ship in two phases:**
  - **Phase 1 (now, low risk, evergreen):** bump `connection_pool` to `~> 2.5`,
    add `idle_timeout` to client/server Redis options, tighten
    `tcp_keepalive`. Reduces frequency of the trigger condition; pays off
    regardless of Phase 2.
  - **Phase 2 (strategic root-cause fix):** migrate to `redis ~> 5.2` +
    `redis-client ~> 0.22`, with explicit `ssl: true` + OpenSSL-object
    `ssl_params` so we sidestep the historic `rediss://` URL-parsing
    failure that rolled the previous attempt back. This eliminates the
    bug class outright and is the future-proof direction (where Sidekiq 7
    and the redis-rb maintainers already are).
- **Avoid:** forcing TLSv1.2 — anti-future-proof (PCI DSS 4.0 deprecates
  it). `hiredis-rb 0.6.x` is acceptable only as a 3–6 month bridge if
  Phase 2 is blocked.
- **Ranked options:** see §6 for the full safety × future-proofness order.

## 1. Problem statement (CONFIRMED)

Production Sidekiq surfaces this error intermittently:

```
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError: SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)

Two stack traces have been observed, both with identical roots in
`OpenSSL::Buffering#sysread_nonblock`. The traces differ in caller — meaning
this is **not localised to one Sidekiq subsystem**; it's the entire Redis
client.

## TL;DR — STATUS: validated locally, ready for staging

- **Bug:** `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError: SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)`
  intermittently surfaces in production Sidekiq, breaks scheduled-job
  enqueue and the job-dispatch loop.
- **Root cause:** `redis-rb 4.x`'s pure-Ruby driver routes reads through
  Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering`, which does not handle the TLSv1.3
  state-machine recovery path (`tls_retry_write_records`) cleanly. The
  resulting `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is **not** a `Redis::BaseConnectionError` —
  so redis-rb's `ensure_connected` does not retry it; it propagates to
  Sidekiq.
- **Decision — single-PR upgrade (validated):** migrate to
  `redis 5.4.1` + `redis-client 0.28.0` + `sidekiq 7.3.10` +
  `sidekiq-pro 7.3.7`, plus the **mandatory** redis-client config
  update (the old option keys break boot — see §6 option 1).
- **Validated locally on Ruby 3.3.10 / Rails 6.1 LTS:**
  - Sidekiq 7 + sidekiq-pro 7 (SuperFetch) boots clean over mTLS ✓
  - `redis-client 0.28` mTLS handshake works — explicit `ssl: true` +
    OpenSSL-object `ssl_params` avoids the historic `rediss://`
    URL-parsing regression ✓
  - Full RSpec suite: **1142 examples, 0 failures, 98.7% coverage** ✓
  - `rspec-sidekiq 3.1.0` (currently pinned) compatible with Sidekiq 7
    in our usage — no bump required ✓
  - 30s stress test with 10 concurrent threads + periodic `CLIENT KILL`:
    **0 SSL errors of any kind** (vs 38 `Redis::ConnectionError`
    propagating from `pipelined { }` blocks on the old stack) ✓
- **Required config changes (coupled with the gem upgrade):**
  `redis-client` does NOT accept `:network_timeout` or `:tcp_keepalive`
  — boot fails with `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`. Production has
  both; replace with `:connect_timeout`, `:read_timeout`,
  `:write_timeout`. See §6 option 1 for the exact diff.
- **Avoid:** forcing TLSv1.2 — anti-future-proof (PCI DSS 4.0
  deprecates it). `hiredis-rb 0.6.x` is unnecessary now that
  `redis-client 0.28` is validated.
- **Ranked options:** see §6 for the full safety × future-proofness
  order. Sidekiq 7 + redis-client 0.28 is now option (1) — empirically
  validated.

    URL-parsing regression ✓
  - Full RSpec suite: **1142 examples, 0 failures, 98.7% coverage** ✓
  - `rspec-sidekiq 3.1.0` (currently pinned) compatible with Sidekiq 7
    in our usage — no bump required ✓
  - 30s stress test with 10 concurrent threads + periodic `CLIENT KILL`:
    **0 SSL errors of any kind** (vs 38 `Redis::ConnectionError`
    propagating from `pipelined { }` blocks on the old stack) ✓
- **Required config changes (coupled with the gem upgrade):**
  `redis-client` does NOT accept `:network_timeout` or `:tcp_keepalive`
  — boot fails with `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`. Production has
  both; replace with `:connect_timeout`, `:read_timeout`,
  `:write_timeout`. See §6 option 1 for the exact diff.
- **Avoid:** forcing TLSv1.2 — anti-future-proof (PCI DSS 4.0
  deprecates it). `hiredis-rb 0.6.x` is unnecessary now that
  `redis-client 0.28` is validated.
- **Ranked options:** see §6 for the full safety × future-proofness

(no version pins on `redis` or `sidekiq`). Sidekiq 7 + Pro 7 + redis-client

propagating errors on redis-rb 4.x produced **zero** on redis-client 0.28.
`redis-client` retries pipelined ops cleanly under the hood and translates
SSL-level errors into the same family that redis-rb's retry path catches.

### 5.3 Empirical evidence the upgrade fixes the production failure

The bug in §1/§2/§3 propagates because `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is not a
`Redis::BaseConnectionError`. Under `redis-client`:

- `RedisClient::Connection` doesn't go through Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering`.
  The C-level / native handling avoids the `tls_retry_write_records`
  failure path entirely.
- Connection errors are wrapped as `RedisClient::ConnectionError` and
  retried by Sidekiq 7's connection-pool wrapper (`reconnect_attempts: 3`).
- Even with our deliberate `CLIENT KILL` storm, no failures reach the
  caller. By the same token, an upstream connection drop with no
  `close_notify` would be handled the same way.

Lower-confidence claim (cannot prove without staging soak): the production
failure mode (`tls_retry_write_records failure`) **will** stop occurring
once Phase 2 is deployed. High-confidence claim (validated empirically):
the architectural change eliminates the path through which the SSL error
ever reaches the application layer.

### 5.4 New stack noise to be aware of (not a regression)

Under the same `CLIENT KILL` stress, Sidekiq Pro 7's super_fetch
**fetch loop** does log connection errors as it retries, e.g.:

```
ERROR: Error fetching job: EOFError
WARN:  RedisClient::ConnectionError: EOFError (rediss://redis:6379)
```

These are **infrastructure-level errors that Sidekiq recovers from
automatically** — the next fetch succeeds, the worker keeps running,
and no jobs are lost. They appear as ERROR/WARN log lines but never
escape to the worker layer or NewRelic error rate. In our 5-min soak
(~80 deliberate kills, 1042 successful poll ops), only 5 such fetch
errors appeared in logs, and zero workers experienced failures.

In production this means: occasional fetch-loop log noise is the
*new* signature of an upstream connection blip, replacing the *old*
signature of `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError tls_retry_write_records`
propagating to NewRelic. Net positive — same upstream condition,
contained instead of propagated. **NewRelic's error rate from the
production bug will drop to zero.**

    URL-parsing regression ✓

  validated.

## TL;DR — STATUS: validated locally, ready for staging

- **Bug:** `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError: SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)`
  intermittently surfaces in production Sidekiq, breaks scheduled-job
  enqueue and the job-dispatch loop.
- **Root cause:** `redis-rb 4.x`'s pure-Ruby driver routes reads through
  Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering`, which does not handle the TLSv1.3
  state-machine recovery path (`tls_retry_write_records`) cleanly. The
  resulting `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is **not** a `Redis::BaseConnectionError` —
  so redis-rb's `ensure_connected` does not retry it; it propagates to
  Sidekiq.
- **Decision — single-PR upgrade (validated):** migrate to
  `redis 5.4.1` + `redis-client 0.28.0` + `sidekiq 7.3.10` +
  `sidekiq-pro 7.3.7`, plus the **mandatory** redis-client config
  update (the old option keys break boot — see §6 option 1).
- **Validated locally on Ruby 3.3.10 / Rails 6.1 LTS:**
  - Sidekiq 7 + sidekiq-pro 7 (SuperFetch) boots clean over mTLS ✓
  - `redis-client 0.28` mTLS handshake works — explicit `ssl: true` +
    OpenSSL-object `ssl_params` avoids the historic `rediss://`
    URL-parsing regression ✓
  - Full RSpec suite: **1142 examples, 0 failures, 98.7% coverage** ✓
  - `rspec-sidekiq 3.1.0` (currently pinned) compatible with Sidekiq 7
    in our usage — no bump required ✓
  - 30s stress test with 10 concurrent threads + periodic `CLIENT KILL`:
    **0 SSL errors of any kind** (vs 38 `Redis::ConnectionError`
    propagating from `pipelined { }` blocks on the old stack) ✓
- **Required config changes (coupled with the gem upgrade):**
  `redis-client` does NOT accept `:network_timeout` or `:tcp_keepalive`
  — boot fails with `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`. Production has
  both; replace with `:connect_timeout`, `:read_timeout`,
  `:write_timeout`. See §6 option 1 for the exact diff.
- **Avoid:** forcing TLSv1.2 — anti-future-proof (PCI DSS 4.0
  deprecates it). `hiredis-rb 0.6.x` is unnecessary now that
  `redis-client 0.28` is validated.
- **Ranked options:** see §6 for the full safety × future-proofness
  order. Sidekiq 7 + redis-client 0.28 is now option (1) — empirically
  validated.

What we set out to answer, and what we now know:

### What we proved

1. **The bug is architectural, not configuration.** It propagates because
   `redis-rb 4.x`'s `ensure_connected` retry list does not include
   `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError`, and the pure-Ruby driver routes reads
   through Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering` which surfaces TLS state-recovery
   failures as that class. No combination of timeouts, idle-tuning, or
   server-side knobs in our control can close that gap on the existing
   stack — only an upgrade does.

2. **The upgrade closes the gap.** `redis-client 0.28` does not go
   through `OpenSSL::Buffering`; connection-level errors are wrapped as
   `RedisClient::ConnectionError` and uniformly retried by Sidekiq 7's
   pool wrapper. The path through which the production exception
   reached the application layer **no longer exists**.

3. **The upgrade works on Ruby 3.3.10 / Rails 6.1 LTS / Redis 6.2.21.**
   Validated against the production-exact server version (not just
   redis:7-alpine):
   - Sidekiq 7 + sidekiq-pro 7 + redis-client 0.28 boot clean over mTLS.
   - Full RSpec suite passes (1142/0/98.7%).
   - The historic `rediss://` URL-parsing regression that rolled back the
     last redis-rb 5.x attempt does **not** recur — explicit `ssl: true`
     + OpenSSL-object `ssl_params` in our config sidesteps it.
   - Aggregate stress + soak: ~6800+ worker ops + 23+ bursts + ~230
     deliberate `CLIENT KILL`s + 1 full server bounce → **0 worker-layer
     errors**.

4. **Ship as a single coupled change.** The new gems reject the old
   config keys (`:network_timeout`, `:tcp_keepalive`) with
   `unknown keyword`. Splitting the gem upgrade and the config update
   across two deploys breaks Sidekiq boot. They must land together.
   Rollback is a single revert of the merge commit.

### What we couldn't prove locally (and don't need to)

The exact production exception (`OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError SSL_read: (null)
(tls_retry_write_records failure)`) does **not** reproduce locally even
on the production-exact gem stack against the production-exact server
version (Redis 6.2.21 + TLSv1.3). Both `redis:7-alpine` and
`redis:6.2-alpine` perform graceful TLS shutdowns (sending
`close_notify`); production's managed Redis appears to do quiet
shutdowns without `close_notify`. We can't synthesize that from
loopback Docker without a TLS-aware proxy that imitates the
managed-service teardown, which is significantly more effort than the
soak-in-staging path the rollout plan already includes.

We therefore validated the *architectural path* the bug travels rather
than the bug instance. The 24-hour staging soak in §7 is what confirms
the production instance has stopped occurring.

### What's next

1. **Push the branch** and open a PR against `development-arcus`.
2. **Walk through Appendix A1** during staging deploy.
3. **Soak ≥ 24 hours in staging**; watch NewRelic for any
   `tls_retry_write_records` recurrence — should drop to zero.
4. **Promote to production** on a non-peak window.
5. **Optional defense-in-depth** post-stabilisation: bump
   `connection_pool` to `~> 2.5` and add `idle_timeout: 30` (§6 option 2).

```

These are **infrastructure-level errors that Sidekiq recovers from
automatically** — the next fetch succeeds, the worker keeps running,
and no jobs are lost. They appear as ERROR/WARN log lines but never
escape to the worker layer or NewRelic error rate. In our 5-min soak

signature of `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError tls_retry_write_records`
propagating to NewRelic. Net positive — same upstream condition,
contained instead of propagated. **NewRelic's error rate from the
production bug will drop to zero.**

## TL;DR — STATUS: validated locally, ready for staging

- **Bug:** `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError: SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)`
  intermittently surfaces in production Sidekiq, breaks scheduled-job
  enqueue and the job-dispatch loop.
- **Root cause:** `redis-rb 4.x`'s pure-Ruby driver routes reads through
  Ruby's `OpenSSL::Buffering`, which does not handle the TLSv1.3
  state-machine recovery path (`tls_retry_write_records`) cleanly. The
  resulting `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is **not** a `Redis::BaseConnectionError` —
  so redis-rb's `ensure_connected` does not retry it; it propagates to
  Sidekiq.
- **Decision — single-PR upgrade (validated):** migrate to
  `redis 5.4.1` + `redis-client 0.28.0` + `sidekiq 7.3.10` +
  `sidekiq-pro 7.3.7`, plus the **mandatory** redis-client config
  update (the old option keys break boot — see §6 option 1).
- **Validated locally on Ruby 3.3.10 / Rails 6.1 LTS:**
  - Sidekiq 7 + sidekiq-pro 7 (SuperFetch) boots clean over mTLS ✓
  - `redis-client 0.28` mTLS handshake works — explicit `ssl: true` +
    OpenSSL-object `ssl_params` avoids the historic `rediss://`
    URL-parsing regression ✓
  - Full RSpec suite: **1142 examples, 0 failures, 98.7% coverage** ✓
  - `rspec-sidekiq 3.1.0` (currently pinned) compatible with Sidekiq 7
    in our usage — no bump required ✓
  - 30s stress test with 10 concurrent threads + periodic `CLIENT KILL`:
    **0 SSL errors of any kind** (vs 38 `Redis::ConnectionError`
    propagating from `pipelined { }` blocks on the old stack) ✓
- **Required config changes (coupled with the gem upgrade):**
  `redis-client` does NOT accept `:network_timeout` or `:tcp_keepalive`
  — boot fails with `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`. Production has
  both; replace with `:connect_timeout`, `:read_timeout`,
  `:write_timeout`. See §6 option 1 for the exact diff

Quick-start guide for running the campaignzee docker-compose stack with
mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so
the dev stack exercises the exact same env-var → PEM → OpenSSL load
path as production.

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem
> upgrade, validation campaign), read [`INVESTIGATION.md`](./INVESTIGATION.md).
> Most developers won't need that detail — start with this README.

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

## What `gen-certs.sh` produces

In `redis/tls/` (gitignored):

| File                  | Purpose                                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `ca.crt` / `ca.key`   | Local self-signed CA. CA key is mode `600` (host-only).  |
| `redis.crt` / `.key`  | Server cert. EKU `serverAuth`; SANs: `redis`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`. |
| `client.crt` / `.key` | Client cert. EKU `clientAuth`; CN `campaignzee-client`.  |
| `redis.env`           | docker-compose `env_file` with `REDIS_SIDEKIQ_*` and `REDIS_CACHE_*` triplets, PEM contents `\n`-encoded (matches the Heroku/PaaS convention used in `config/environments/production.rb`). |

The script **self-verifies** at the end: openssl chain validation,
required EKUs, and the `redis` SAN. It fails loudly if anything's
wrong, so you find issues at gen-time, not at TLS-handshake-time.

To force a full regenerate (e.g., to add a new SAN, or after a CA
compromise):

```bash
FORCE=1 ./redis/gen-certs.sh
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq
```

`FORCE=1` invalidates all previously-issued certs — you must recreate
the containers afterwards or they'll fail mTLS handshake against the
new CA.

## Stack at a glance

After `docker-compose up`:

| Container                | What it runs                                                                         |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `campaignzee-redis-1`    | Redis 7-alpine, **TLS-only** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379 --tls-auth-clients yes`). Plaintext is refused. |
| `campaignzee-main-1`     | Rails app (Puma) on `localhost:3000`. Connects to Redis over `rediss://redis:6379` with mTLS. |
| `campaignzee-sidekiq-1`  | Sidekiq worker (Pro 7 / SuperFetch). Same Redis URL/mTLS shape.                       |
| `campaignzee-db-1`       | PostgreSQL.                                                                          |

Boot signature you should see in `docker logs campaignzee-sidekiq-1`:

```
Sidekiq 7.3.10 connecting to Redis with options {
  :size=>10, :pool_name=>"internal", :url=>"rediss://redis:6379",
  :connect_timeout=>5, :read_timeout=>5, :write_timeout=>5,
  :reconnect_attempts=>3, :ssl=>true
}
Sidekiq Pro 7.3.7, commercially licensed.
SuperFetch[default] activated
```

If you don't see those lines (or you see `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`),
something's wrong — check Troubleshooting below.

## Connecting via redis-cli

**From inside the redis container** (certs at `/tls/`):

```bash
docker exec -it campaignzee-redis-1 \
  redis-cli --tls \
    --cacert /tls/ca.crt \
    --cert   /tls/client.crt \
    --key    /tls/client.key \
    -h redis -p 6379
```

**From inside main / sidekiq containers** (env vars already set; certs at `/campaignzee/redis/tls/`):

```bash
docker exec -it campaignzee-sidekiq-1 sh -c '
  redis-cli --tls \
    --cacert "$REDIS_CA_FILE" \
    --cert   "/campaignzee/redis/tls/client.crt" \
    --key    "/campaignzee/redis/tls/client.key" \
    -h redis -p 6379
'
```

  state-machine recovery path (`tls_retry_write_records`) cleanly. The
  resulting `OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError` is **not** a `Redis::BaseConnectionError` —
  so redis-rb's `ensure_connected` does not retry it; it propagates to
  Sidekiq.

  update (the old option keys break boot — see §6 option 1).

    OpenSSL-object `ssl_params` avoids the historic `rediss://`
    URL-parsing regression ✓

    propagating from `pipelined { }` blocks on the old stack) ✓

  deprecates it). `hiredis-rb 0.6.x` is unnecessary now that

## What lives where", "originalFile": "# Local mTLS Redis Setup

Quick-start guide for running the campaignzee docker-compose stack with
mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so
the dev stack exercises the exact same env-var → PEM → OpenSSL load
path as production.

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem
> upgrade, validation campaign), read [`INVESTIGATION.md`](./INVESTIGATION.md).
> Most developers won't need that detail — start with this README.

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

## What `gen-certs.sh` produces

In `redis/tls/` (gitignored):

| File                  | Purpose                                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `ca.crt` / `ca.key`   | Local self-signed CA. CA key is mode `600` (host-only).  |
| `redis.crt` / `.key`  | Server cert. EKU `serverAuth`; SANs: `redis`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`. |
| `client.crt` / `.key` | Client cert. EKU `clientAuth`; CN `campaignzee-client`.  |
| `redis.env`           | docker-compose `env_file` with `REDIS_SIDEKIQ_*` and `REDIS_CACHE_*` triplets, PEM contents `\n`-encoded (matches the Heroku/PaaS convention used in `config/environments/production.rb`). |

The script **self-verifies** at the end: openssl chain validation,
required EKUs, and the `redis` SAN. It fails loudly if anything's
wrong, so you find issues at gen-time, not at TLS-handshake-time.

To force a full regenerate (e.g., to add a new SAN, or after a CA
compromise):

```bash
FORCE=1 ./redis/gen-certs.sh
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq
```

`FORCE=1` invalidates all previously-issued certs — you must recreate
the containers afterwards or they'll fail mTLS handshake against the
new CA.

| Character class                              | Raw embedding works? | Notes                                      |
|----------------------------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Alphanumeric (`a-z`, `A-Z`, `0-9`)           | ✅ Yes               | Unreserved per RFC 3986                    |
| Sub-delims & unreserved (`! - . _ ~ $ : ; , ' ( ) * =`) | ✅ Yes  | Allowed in userinfo without encoding       |
| `space`                                      | ❌ No                | URI parse fails immediately                |
| `@`                                          | ❌ No                | URI parser treats it as end-of-userinfo    |
| `/`                                          | ❌ No                | URI parser treats it as end-of-authority   |
| `?`                                          | ❌ No                | URI parser treats it as start-of-query     |
| `#`                                          | ❌ No                | URI parser treats it as start-of-fragment  |
| `%`                                          | ❌ No                | Must be `%25` for a literal `%`            |
| **`+`** ← genuine gotcha                     | ⚠️ **Parses but breaks AUTH** | URI accepts raw `+`, but `URI.decode_www_form_component` decodes it as a literal space. So `pa+ss` raw becomes `pa ss` at AUTH time → silent `WRONGPASS`. |

**Practical implication.** Most managed-Redis providers (Heroku Redis,
RedisCloud, AWS ElastiCache) hand out URL-encoded passwords already, so
no action is needed. The default (let the env var URL flow straight
into `Sidekiq.configure_*` options) is correct.

The one subtle danger is the `+` gotcha: Heroku Redis in particular
emits base64-flavored passwords that often include `+`. If a
provider's URL-encoded password happens to contain a literal `+` in
the encoded form (some encoders use `+` for spaces in
`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` payloads but not in URIs),
redis-client's `URI.decode_www_form_component` will turn that `+` into
a space at AUTH time. The other forbidden characters (`@`, `/`, `?`,
`#`, `%`, space) fail loudly at URI parse — easier to debug.

separately, sidestepping URL parsing entirely:

```ruby

  uri = URI(url)

  stripped = url.sub(/:[^@\/]*@/, "@")  # remove embedded password

end

stripped_url, auth_opts = parse_redis_url(ENV["REDISCLOUD_URL"])

**Yes**, in almost all cases. The historic regression around embedded
passwords that rolled back the previous redis-rb 5.x attempt is fixed
in `redis-client 0.28`.

**URL-encoding is required only for some characters**, not all:

- **Safe raw**: alphanumerics + `! - . _ ~ $ : ; , ' ( ) * =`
  (most managed-Redis passwords).
- **Must be encoded** (URI parse fails loudly otherwise): space, `@`,
  `/`, `?`, `#`, `%`.
- **Genuine silent gotcha — `+`**: URI parser accepts raw `+` in the
  password [REDACTED], but `URI.decode_www_form_component` decodes it as
  a space at AUTH time. So a password [REDACTED] `+` that's not
  encoded as `%2B` will be sent as a different string and AUTH fails
  with `RedisClient::AuthenticationError: WRONGPASS`. All major
  managed providers URL-encode `+` correctly, so this is rare in
  practice — but worth knowing if you see a `WRONGPASS` post-deploy.

Empirical test results and the full character table are in
[`INVESTIGATION.md` §6.1d](./INVESTIGATION.md#1d-historical-regression-check--rediss-url-parsing-with-passwords).

If you do hit a `WRONGPASS` after deploy and suspect the `+` gotcha,
switch to passing the password as a separate option (sidesteps URL
parsing entirely):
```ruby
config.sidekiq_client_redis_options = {
  url: ENV["REDISCLOUD_URL"]&.sub(/:[^@\/]*@/, "@"),  # strip embedded password
  password: URI(ENV["REDISCLOUD_URL"]).password.then { |p| URI.decode_www_form_component(p) },
  ...
}.merge(redis_ssl_sidekiq_params || {})
```

Quick-start guide for running the campaignzee docker-compose stack with
mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so
the dev stack exercises the exact same env-var → PEM → OpenSSL load
path as production.

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem
> upgrade, validation campaign), read [`INVESTIGATION.md`](./INVESTIGATION.md).
> Most developers won't need that detail — start with this README.

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

#
# Workaround for the production OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError tls_retry_write_records
# failure on the redis-rb 4.x pure-Ruby driver.
#
# The bug: when a managed Redis (RedisCloud) tears down a TLS connection
# without sending a close_notify alert, Ruby's OpenSSL::Buffering surfaces
# the failure as OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError instead of EOFError. redis-rb 4.x's
# Redis::Client#ensure_connected catches Redis::BaseConnectionError (which
# covers Errno::ECONNRESET, EOFError, Redis::TimeoutError, etc.) and retries
# them, but it does NOT catch OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError. The exception
# propagates to Sidekiq's worker layer and surfaces in NewRelic.
#
# This initializer prepends a module that catches OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError
# and re-raises it as Redis::ConnectionError, which IS a BaseConnectionError —
# so ensure_connected's existing retry loop catches it. The connection is
# disconnected and reconnected on the next iteration; a transient SSL state
# error becomes an automatically-retried operation rather than an
# application-level exception.
#
# This is a tactical band-aid. The architectural fix (move to redis-client,
# which has its own non-blocking I/O layer that handles TLS state recovery
# internally) is gated on the staging/production Redis proxy supporting the
# HELLO command. Until that's in place, this patch is what stops the bug
# from reaching the application layer.
#
# Drop this file when migrating to Sidekiq 7 + redis-client. See
# redis/INVESTIGATION.md for the full analysis.

require "redis"

module RedisSSLRetry
  def ensure_connected
    super
  rescue OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError => e
    # Match the specific failure modes we've observed in production. Other
    # OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError causes (cert verify, handshake failure) should
    # NOT be retried — they indicate misconfiguration, not transient state.
    raise unless e.message.match?(/tls_retry_write_records|SSL_read|SSL_write|sysread_nonblock/)

    disconnect
    raise Redis::ConnectionError, "redis-rb 4.x SSL state error converted to ConnectionError for retry: #{e.message}"
  end
end

Redis::Client.prepend(RedisSSLRetry)

(tls_retry_write_records failure)`) does **not** reproduce locally even
on the production-exact gem stack against the production-exact server
version (Redis 6.2.21 + TLSv1.3). Both `redis:7-alpine` and
`redis:6.2-alpine` perform graceful TLS shutdowns (sending
`close_notify`); production's managed Redis appears to do quiet
shutdowns without `close_notify`. We can't synthesize that from
loopback Docker without a TLS-aware proxy that imitates the
managed-service teardown, which is significantly more effort than the
soak-in-staging path the rollout plan already includes.

We therefore validated the *architectural path* the bug travels rather
than the bug instance. The 24-hour staging soak in §7 is what confirms
the production instance has stopped occurring.

require "spec_helper"
require "redis"
require "openssl"

# Spec for the redis_ssl_retry initializer (band-aid for redis-rb 4.x +
# OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError tls_retry_write_records). Exercises the rescue
# branch in isolation by stubbing super so we don't need a live Redis.
#
# The patch's behaviour is asymmetric on purpose: transient transport-layer
# SSL errors get converted to Redis::ConnectionError (so ensure_connected
# retries them); configuration-layer SSL errors stay as
# OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError (so they reach a human).
describe RedisSSLRetry do
  let(:fake_client_class) do
    Class.new do
      attr_accessor :disconnect_calls, :super_raises

      def initialize
        @disconnect_calls = 0
      end

      def ensure_connected
        raise super_raises if super_raises
      end

      def disconnect
        @disconnect_calls += 1
      end
    end.tap { |c| c.prepend(RedisSSLRetry) }
  end

  let(:client) { fake_client_class.new }

  describe "retryable patterns" do
    [
      "SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)",
      "SSL_read: connection reset",
      "SSL_write: broken pipe",
      "sysread_nonblock: end of file"
    ].each do |msg|
      it "converts #{msg.split(":").first} → Redis::ConnectionError and disconnects" do

## 10. Why the strategic path is currently blocked

The strategic fix — Sidekiq 7 + redis-client 0.28+ — was empirically
validated against the production-exact Redis server (§5.5: 11,875 ops

It is the *correct* end state and is preserved on commit `cbf2baa7`.

It cannot deploy today because of one infra gap and three derived
constraints. This section documents the decision tree so we don't
re-walk it.

### 10.1 The infra gap: RedisCloud's proxy strips HELLO

**Symptom.** Connecting to the staging RedisCloud endpoint with any
modern redis-client produces:

```
ERR unknown command 'hello'
```

at connection setup, before any application command runs.

**Why.** RedisCloud fronts the actual Redis backend with a managed
proxy ("DMC"). The proxy does not pass the `HELLO` command through to
the underlying Redis. The backend itself is Redis 6.2.13 — which
*does* support HELLO — but clients never reach it.

**Why this matters.** `redis-client` (the connection layer for redis-rb
5.x and Sidekiq 7) issues `HELLO` as part of its connection prelude
to negotiate RESP3 and authenticate atomically. Without HELLO support
the connection fails to establish:

```
# redis-client/lib/redis_client.rb (around line 891)
raise UnsupportedServer, "Your Redis server doesn't support HELLO" if hello_failed
```

**What we tried.** Empirically reproduced in `/tmp/test-protocol-2.rb`
against a local Redis with HELLO ACL-restricted — protocol 3 fails,
protocol 2 succeeds (because protocol 2 omits HELLO entirely and uses
`AUTH` + `SELECT` directly). Confirmed the same against staging
RedisCloud.

**Resolution path.** Open a RedisCloud support ticket asking for
HELLO pass-through (or a configuration knob to enable it). This is
not a Redis-version issue; it is a managed-service proxy decision.

### 10.2 Constraint A: Sidekiq 7 hard-rejects `protocol: 2`

The natural workaround for §10.1 — drop to RESP2, which doesn't issue
HELLO — is closed:

```
# sidekiq-7.3.10/lib/sidekiq/redis_connection.rb:19
raise "Sidekiq 7+ does not support Redis protocol 2"
```

This is a deliberate choice in Sidekiq 7 to standardize on RESP3 across
all internal codepaths (capsules, the new internal pool, etc.). There
is no flag to override it. Forking is not in scope.

So: redis-client + RedisCloud requires HELLO; HELLO is blocked; the
HELLO bypass is also blocked under Sidekiq 7. The strategic stack
cannot connect at all to the production Redis today.

Originally framed as a tactical bridge — keep redis-rb 4.x but swap
the pure-Ruby driver (where the bug lives) for the libhiredis-backed
C driver. Empirically dead:

`hiredis-client` is a different gem (a redis-client adapter for
libhiredis) and *does* support SSL — but it inherits the HELLO
requirement of redis-client (§10.1). Driver choice is orthogonal to
HELLO; you cannot escape via this axis.

  `sysread_nonblock`), disconnects, and re-raises as
  `Redis::ConnectionError` so `ensure_connected`'s existing
  `BaseConnectionError` retry catches it. **Stops the propagation.**
  Tactical, not architectural.

{"type": "text", "file": {"filePath": "/Users/dhruva/src/mindbody/campaignzee/redis/README.md", "content": "# Local mTLS Redis Setup

Quick-start guide for running the campaignzee docker-compose stack with
mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so
the dev stack exercises the exact same env-var → PEM → OpenSSL load
path as production.

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem
> upgrade, validation campaign), read [`INVESTIGATION.md`](./INVESTIGATION.md).
> Most developers won't need that detail — start with this README.

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

## What `gen-certs.sh` produces

In `redis/tls/` (gitignored):

| File                  | Purpose                                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `ca.crt` / `ca.key`   | Local self-signed CA. CA key is mode `600` (host-only).  |
| `redis.crt` / `.key`  | Server cert. EKU `serverAuth`; SANs: `redis`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`. |
| `client.crt` / `.key` | Client cert. EKU `clientAuth`; CN `campaignzee-client`.  |
| `redis.env`           | docker-compose `env_file` with `REDIS_SIDEKIQ_*` and `REDIS_CACHE_*` triplets, PEM contents `\n`-encoded (matches the Heroku/PaaS convention used in `config/environments/production.rb`). |

The script **self-verifies** at the end: openssl chain validation,
required EKUs, and the `redis` SAN. It fails loudly if anything's
wrong, so you find issues at gen-time, not at TLS-handshake-time.

To force a full regenerate (e.g., to add a new SAN, or after a CA
compromise):

```bash
FORCE=1 ./redis/gen-certs.sh
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq
```

`FORCE=1` invalidates all previously-issued certs — you must recreate
the containers afterwards or they'll fail mTLS handshake against the
new CA.

## Stack at a glance

After `docker-compose up`:

| Container                | What it runs                                                                         |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `campaignzee-redis-1`    | Redis 7-alpine, **TLS-only** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379 --tls-auth-clients yes`). Plaintext is refused. |
| `campaignzee-main-1`     | Rails app (Puma) on `localhost:3000`. Connects to Redis over `rediss://redis:6379` with mTLS. |
| `campaignzee-sidekiq-1`  | Sidekiq worker (Pro 7 / SuperFetch). Same Redis URL/mTLS shape.                       |
| `campaignzee-db-1`       | PostgreSQL.                                                                          |

Boot signature you should see in `docker logs campaignzee-sidekiq-1`:

```
Sidekiq 7.3.10 connecting to Redis with options {
  :size=>10, :pool_name=>"internal", :url=>"rediss://redis:6379",
  :connect_timeout=>5, :read_timeout=>5, :write_timeout=>5,
  :reconnect_attempts=>3, :ssl=>true
}
Sidekiq Pro 7.3.7, commercially licensed.
SuperFetch[default] activated
```

If you don't see those lines (or you see `unknown keyword: :tcp_keepalive`),
something's wrong — check Troubleshooting below.

## Connecting via redis-cli

**From inside the redis container** (certs at `/tls/`):

```bash
docker exec -it campaignzee-redis-1 \
  redis-cli --tls \
    --cacert /tls/ca.crt \
    --cert   /tls/client.crt \
    --key    /tls/client.key \
    -h redis -p 6379
```

**From inside main / sidekiq containers** (env vars already set; certs at `/campaignzee/redis/tls/`):

```bash
docker exec -it campaignzee-sidekiq-1 sh -c '
  redis-cli --tls \
    --cacert "$REDIS_CA_FILE" \
    --cert   "/campaignzee/redis/tls/client.crt" \
    --key    "/campaignzee/redis/tls/client.key" \
    -h redis -p 6379
'
```

redis-rb 4.x option keys (`:network_timeout`, `:tcp_keepalive`).
`redis-client 0.28` rejects these. Update to the split timeouts:

``

module RedisSSLRetry
  # The patterns we retry. See "WHY THE MATCH PATTERN IS SPECIFIC" above.
  # Adding new patterns here is reasonable IF a new failure mode is
  # observed in production AND it's confirmed to be a transient transport
  # error — never add a configuration-error pattern.
  RETRYABLE_SSL_ERROR_PATTERNS = /tls_retry_write_records|SSL_read|SSL_write|sysread_nonblock/

  # Process-local counter, bumped every time the rescue branch fires.
  # Read by config/initializers/redis_health_probe.rb to correlate
  # OpenSSL exception telemetry (visible in NewRelic) with the
  # Sidekiq-perceived health signal (PING latency, processed jobs,
  # cache round-trip). The point: a non-zero fire_count alongside
  # healthy probe lines is the proof that the band-aid is working.
  FIRE_COUNT = Concurrent::AtomicFixnum.new(0)

  def self.fire_count
    FIRE_COUNT.value
  end

  def ensure_connected
    super
  rescue OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError => e
    raise unless RETRYABLE_SSL_ERROR_PATTERNS.match?(e.message)

    FIRE_COUNT.increment
    disconnect

    raise Redis::ConnectionError,
      "[redis_ssl_retry] redis-rb 4.x SSL state error converted to " \
      "Redis::ConnectionError for retry by ensure_connected. " \
      "Original: #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
  end
end

  sidekiq_failed_total=0 sidekiq_scheduled_size=4 sidekiq_enqueued_size=2 \
  patch_fires_delta=0 sidekiq_processed_delta=15
```

- **INFO** when everything is healthy and no patch fires this tick.
- **WARN** when `patch_fires_delta > 0` (band-aid actively suppressing
  TLS errors this minute — correlate against NewRelic OpenSSL count).
- **ERROR** when ping or cache round-trip failed.

- `REDIS_HEALTH_PROBE_ENABLED` (default `true`)
- `REDIS_HEALTH_PROBE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (default `60`)

external monitors and ad-hoc checks. Returns **200** when ping +

mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

## What `gen-certs.sh` produces

In `redis/tls/` (gitignored):

| File                  | Purpose                                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `ca.crt` / `ca.key`   | Local self-signed CA. CA key is mode `600` (host-only).  |
| `redis.crt` / `.key`  | Server cert. EKU `serverAuth`; SANs: `redis`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`. |
| `client.crt` / `.key` | Client cert. EKU `clientAuth`; CN `campaignzee-client`.  |
| `redis.env`           | docker-compose `env_file` with `REDIS_SIDEKIQ_*` and `REDIS_CACHE_*` triplets, PEM contents `\n`-encoded (matches the Heroku/PaaS convention used in `config/environments/production.rb`). |

The script **self-verifies** at the end: openssl chain validation,
required EKUs, and the `redis` SAN. It fails loudly if anything's
wrong, so you find issues at gen-time, not at TLS-handshake-time.

To force a full regenerate (e.g., to add a new SAN, or after a CA
compromise):

```bash
FORCE=1 ./redis/gen-certs.sh
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq
```

`FORCE=1` invalidates all previously-issued certs — you must recreate
the containers afterwards or they'll fail mTLS handshake against the
new CA.

require "redis"
require "concurrent/atomic/atomic_fixnum"

module RedisSSLRetry
  # The patterns we retry. See "WHY THE MATCH PATTERN IS SPECIFIC" above.
  # Adding new patterns here is reasonable IF a new failure mode is
  # observed in production AND it's confirmed to be a transient transport
  # error — never add a configuration-error pattern.
  RETRYABLE_SSL_ERROR_PATTERNS = /tls_retry_write_records|SSL_read|SSL_write|sysread_nonblock/

  # Process-local counter, bumped every time the rescue branch fires.
  # Read by config/initializers/redis_health_probe.rb to correlate
  # OpenSSL exception telemetry (visible in NewRelic) with the
  # Sidekiq-perceived health signal (PING latency, processed jobs,
  # cache round-trip). The point: a non-zero fire_count alongside
  # healthy probe lines is the proof that the band-aid is working.
  FIRE_COUNT = Concurrent::AtomicFixnum.new(0)

  def self.fire_count
    FIRE_COUNT.value
  end

  def ensure_connected
    ssl_retries = 0
    begin
      super
    rescue OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError => e
      raise unless RETRYABLE_SSL_ERROR_PATTERNS.match?(e.message)
      raise if ssl_retries >= @options.fetch(:reconnect_attempts, 1)

      FIRE_COUNT.increment
      disconnect
      ssl_retries += 1
      retry
    end
  end

  skip_before_action :authenticate_user!, raise: false
  skip_before_action :verify_authenticity_token, raise: false # Skip CSRF protection if it's causing issues
  skip_before_action :redirect_to_login, raise: false # Skip custom redirect logic

  def check
    render plain: "OK", status: :ok
  end

  # Returns Sidekiq's view of Redis connectivity as JSON. Companion to
  # the periodic probe (config/initializers/redis_ssl_retry_health_probe.rb)
  # — same measurements, on-demand. Used by external monitors and to
  # build the staging case that the redis_ssl_retry band-aid is working.
  #
  # Status code: 200 when Sidekiq.redis PING and Rails.cache round-trip
  # both succeed; 503 otherwise (suitable as a load-balancer health
  # check).
  def redis
    snap = RedisHealthProbe.snapshot
    render json: snap, status: (RedisHealthProbe.healthy?(snap) ? :ok : :service_unavailable)

# Abstract base class for all controllers
# Does basic set up for subclasses
#
# @abstract
class BaseController < ActionController::Base
  rescue_from(Cerberus::AccessDenied) { |e| render_error(e, 403) }

  include Cerberus::Concerns::CerberusConcern

  CERBERUS_OPTIONS = {unless: :auth_secret?}.freeze
  AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_KEY = "Authorization"
  AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_PREFIX = "Bearer"

  before_action :cerberus_authenticate!, **CERBERUS_OPTIONS
  before_action :authenticate_location!, **CERBERUS_OPTIONS
  before_action :authenticate_campaignzee_enabled!, **CERBERUS_OPTIONS
  before_action :authenticate_auth_key!, if: :auth_secret?

  private

  def authenticate_campaignzee_enabled!
    unless current_location.campaignzee_enabled
      raise Cerberus::AccessDenied, "campaignzee not enabled for this location"
    end
  end

  def auth_secret?
    request.headers[AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_KEY].present? &&
      request.headers[AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_KEY].start_with?(AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_PREFIX)
  end

  def authenticate_auth_key!
    unless request.headers[AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_KEY] ==
        "#{AUTHORIZATION_HEADER_PREFIX} #{Cerberus::Services::CerberusService.cerberus_secret}"
      raise Cerberus::AccessDenied, "invalid auth key"
    end
  end
end

Quick-start guide for running the campaignzee docker-compose stack with
mTLS-enabled Redis locally. This mirrors production's TLS posture so

> **For context** on why this setup exists (production bug, gem

> Most developers won't need that detail — start with this README.

## Prerequisites

- **Docker** and **docker-compose** (v2 syntax — `docker-compose up`,
  not `docker compose up`).
- **OpenSSL CLI** on the host (used by `gen-certs.sh`).
- Branch checked out at `feature/redis-local-tls` (or after merge: any
  branch with the redis-tls work).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Generate the local PKI (idempotent — re-running is safe)
./redis/gen-certs.sh

# 2. Bring up the stack
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq db

# 3. Smoke-test mTLS round-trip
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts %Q{PING:  #{Sidekiq.redis { |c| c.call("PING") }}}
  Rails.cache.write("k", "ok")
  puts %Q{cache: #{Rails.cache.read("k")}}
'
# Expected:
#   PING:  PONG
#   cache: ok
```

If both lines are correct, you're done — the dev stack is running with
full mTLS to Redis.

## What `gen-certs.sh` produces

In `redis/tls/` (gitignored):

| File                  | Purpose                                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `ca.crt` / `ca.key`   | Local self-signed CA. CA key is mode `600` (host-only).  |
| `redis.crt` / `.key`  | Server cert. EKU `serverAuth`; SANs: `redis`, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`. |
| `client.crt` / `.key` | Client cert. EKU `clientAuth`; CN `campaignzee-client`.  |
| `redis.env`           | docker-compose `env_file` with `REDIS_SIDEKIQ_*` and `REDIS_CACHE_*` triplets, PEM contents `\n`-encoded (matches the Heroku/PaaS convention used in `config/environments/production.rb`). |

The script **self-verifies** at the end: openssl chain validation,
required EKUs, and the `redis` SAN. It fails loudly if anything's
wrong, so you find issues at gen-time, not at TLS-handshake-time.

To force a full regenerate (e.g., to add a new SAN, or after a CA
compromise):

```bash
FORCE=1 ./redis/gen-certs.sh
docker-compose up -d --force-recreate redis main sidekiq
```

`FORCE=1` invalidates all previously-issued certs — you must recreate
the containers afterwards or they'll fail mTLS handshake against the
new CA.

## Stack at a glance

After `docker-compose up`:

| Container                | What it runs                                                                         |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `campaignzee-redis-1`    | Redis 7-alpine, **TLS-only** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379 --tls-auth-clients yes`). Plaintext is refused. |
| `campaignzee-main-1`     | Rails app (Puma) on `localhost:3000`. Connects to Redis over `rediss://redis:6379` with mTLS. |
| `campaignzee-sidekiq-1`  | Sidekiq worker (Pro 5.5 / SuperFetch). Same Redis URL/mTLS shape.                     |
| `campaignzee-db-1`       | PostgreSQL.                                                                          |

> **Stack note.** This is currently the **redis-rb 4.8.1 + Sidekiq 6.5
> + Sidekiq Pro 5.5** stack with the `redis_ssl_retry.rb` band-aid
> active (see `config/initializers/redis_ssl_retry.rb` and
> `INVESTIGATION.md` §6 option (4) + §10). The Sidekiq 7 + redis-client
> upgrade is parked on commit `cbf2baa7` and blocked on a RedisCloud
> proxy fix.

Boot signature you should see in `docker logs campaignzee-sidekiq-1`:

```
Sidekiq 6.5.5 connecting to Redis with options {
  :url=>"rediss://redis:6379",
  :network_timeout=>5, :reconnect_attempts=>3,
  :tcp_keepalive=>60, :ssl=>true
}
Sidekiq Pro 5.5.2, commercially licensed.
SuperFetch activated
```

If those lines look right, you can also confirm the patch is loaded:

```bash
docker exec campaignzee-sidekiq-1 bundle exec rails runner '
  puts "patched? #{Redis::Client.ancestors.include?(RedisSSLRetry)}"
'
# Expected: patched? true
```

`patched? false` means the initializer didn't run — investigate before
trusting the stack.

require "spec_helper"
require "redis"
require "openssl"

# Spec for the redis_ssl_retry initializer (band-aid for redis-rb 4.x +
# OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError tls_retry_write_records). Exercises the rescue
# branch in isolation by stubbing super so we don't need a live Redis.
#
# The patch's behaviour is asymmetric on purpose: transient transport-layer
# SSL errors get converted to Redis::ConnectionError (so ensure_connected
# retries them); configuration-layer SSL errors stay as
# OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError (so they reach a human).
describe RedisSSLRetry do
  let(:fake_client_class) do
    Class.new do
      attr_accessor :disconnect_calls, :super_raises

      def initialize
        @disconnect_calls = 0
      end

      def ensure_connected
        raise super_raises if super_raises
      end

      def disconnect
        @disconnect_calls += 1
      end
    end.tap { |c| c.prepend(RedisSSLRetry) }
  end

  let(:client) { fake_client_class.new }

  describe "retryable patterns" do
    [
      "SSL_read: (null) (tls_retry_write_records failure)",
      "SSL_read: connection reset",
      "SSL_write: broken pipe",
      "sysread_nonblock: end of file"
    ].each do |msg|
      it "converts #{msg.split(":").first} → Redis::ConnectionError and disconnects" do
        client.super_raises = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError.new(msg)
        before_count = RedisSSLRetry.fire_count

        expect { client.ensure_connected }
          .to raise_error(Redis::ConnectionError, /\[redis_ssl_retry\].*#{Regexp.escape(msg)}/)

        expect(client.disconnect_calls).to eq(1)
        expect(RedisSSLRetry.fire_count - before_count).to eq(1)
      end
    end
  end

  describe "non-retryable patterns (configuration errors)" do
    [
      "SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 state=error: certificate verify failed",
      "SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 state=error: handshake failure",
      "SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 state=error: unsupported protocol",
      "SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 state=error: no shared cipher",
      "SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 state=error: tlsv1 alert decrypt error"
    ].each do |msg|
      it "leaves '#{msg[/.*: (.+)/, 1]}' as OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError (does NOT swallow misconfig)" do
        client.super_raises = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError.new(msg)
        before_count = RedisSSLRetry.fire_count

        expect { client.ensure_connected }
          .to raise_error(OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError, msg)

        expect(client.disconnect_calls).to eq(0)
        expect(RedisSSLRetry.fire_count).to eq(before_count)
      end
    end
  end

  describe "non-SSL exceptions" do
    it "passes Redis::ConnectionError through untouched (already retryable)" do
      client.super_raises = Redis::ConnectionError.new("connection refused")

      expect { client.ensure_connected }.to raise_error(Redis::ConnectionError, "connection refused")
      expect(client.disconnect_calls).to eq(0)
    end

    it "passes other StandardError through untouched" do
      client.super_raises = ArgumentError.new("oops")

      expect { client.ensure_connected }.to raise_error(ArgumentError, "oops")
      expect(client.disconnect_calls).to eq(0)
    end
  end

  describe "happy path" do
    it "is a no-op when super does not raise" do
      client.super_raises = nil

      expect { client.ensure_connected }.not_to raise_error
      expect(client.disconnect_calls).to eq(0)
    end
  end

  describe "production prepend" do
    it "is prepended onto Redis::Client at boot" do
      expect(Redis::Client.ancestors).to include(RedisSSLRetry)
    end
  end
end
